sections.title: Article 410 Scope — Luminaires, Lampholders, and Lamps
sections.text: Article 410 covers luminaires (light fixtures), lampholders, pendants, incandescent filament lamps, arc lamps, electric discharge lamps, decorative lighting products, and all wiring and equipment forming part of such products or installations. Luminaires must be listed and labeled for their intended use and environment (dry, damp, or wet locations). Installation must comply with the luminaire's listing and the manufacturer's instructions.

sections.title: Listing Requirements for Luminaires
sections.text: All luminaires and lampholders must be listed. Luminaires installed in wet locations must be listed for wet locations and marked 'Suitable for Wet Locations.' Luminaires in damp locations (covered porches, under canopies, carports) must be listed for damp or wet locations and marked 'Suitable for Damp Locations.' A luminaire marked only for dry locations cannot be installed in damp or wet areas. Listed luminaires are typically marked with UL, ETL, CSA, or similar third-party listing marks.

sections.title: Special Location Requirements — Bathtubs, Shower Stalls, Pools
sections.text: In bathtub and shower areas, no part of cord-connected luminaires, hanging luminaires, lighting track, pendants, or ceiling fans shall be located within a zone measured 3 feet horizontally and 8 feet vertically from the top of the bathtub rim or shower stall threshold. Luminaires within this zone must be listed for damp locations (or wet locations if subject to shower spray). GFCI protection is required for all luminaires within 6 feet of the edge of a bathtub or shower stall.

sections.title: Recessed Luminaires — Clearance and Thermal Protection
sections.text: Recessed luminaires must not be installed in direct contact with thermal insulation unless listed for that purpose (marked 'IC' for insulation contact). Non-IC-rated recessed luminaires must maintain a minimum 3-inch clearance from insulation and a minimum 0.5-inch clearance from combustible materials. Recessed luminaires must be thermally protected unless the fixture is labeled Type IC. Installation above suspended ceilings requires the fixture to be listed for installation in contact with insulation if insulation will be placed above the plenum.

sections.title: Luminaires in Clothes Closets
sections.text: Only surface-mounted or recessed incandescent (not allowed due to closet clearance requirements — see below), fluorescent, or LED luminaires with completely enclosed light sources are permitted in clothes closets. Permitted locations: surface-mounted or recessed luminaires on the ceiling if there is a minimum 12-inch clearance horizontally from the nearest point of the storage space. Surface-mounted fluorescent or LED on the wall above the door are permitted only if there is a minimum 6-inch clearance from storage. Completely enclosed luminaires must be used to prevent ignition of stored materials.

sections.title: Track Lighting — Power and Loading
sections.text: Track lighting must be installed so that the maximum load on any 1-foot section of track does not exceed the ratings of the section. The total connected load of track lighting must not exceed the current rating of the branch circuit to which the track is connected. Luminaires on track may not be installed within the zone of a bathtub or shower. Track lighting in other areas must have a grounding conductor. The total wattage of luminaires on a track must be calculated at 150% of actual load for branch circuit sizing.

sections.title: Luminaires Connected to Branch Circuits
sections.text: Branch circuits for lighting must comply with Article 210. Each luminaire must be connected to a grounded (neutral) conductor and an ungrounded (hot) conductor. The switch controlling a luminaire must be in the ungrounded (hot) conductor only. Luminaires must not be used to supply loads other than lighting unless the luminaire is specifically designed and marked for additional loads. The weight of a luminaire must not exceed the box or support capacity.

sections.title: Article 700 Scope — Emergency Systems
sections.text: Article 700 covers electrical safety and emergency operations of electrical systems, circuits, and equipment installed for illumination or power in the event the normal supply fails. Emergency systems must supply power to exit lights, emergency lighting, fire detection and alarm systems, public address systems, and other systems required for evacuation. Emergency systems must be legally required by municipal, state, federal, or other codes. Legally Required Standby Systems (Article 701) and Optional Standby Systems (Article 702) are separate categories.

sections.title: Emergency Power Sources
sections.text: Acceptable power sources for emergency systems include: (1) storage batteries (lead acid, nickel-cadmium, lithium, or other approved type) that automatically provide power with no delay, (2) generator sets driven by prime movers — must start and transfer load within 10 seconds, (3) uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) that provide immediate power and sustain for required duration, (4) self-contained unit equipment (battery packs) listed to UL 924. Central battery systems must supply all emergency loads for at least 1.5 hours (90 minutes). Unit equipment battery packs must supply the connected load for at least 1.5 hours.

sections.title: Emergency Lighting Equipment
sections.text: Unit equipment (emergency battery packs) must be permanently fixed in place, with batteries and lamps of the same type, have sufficient wattage to maintain required illumination for 1.5 hours, have an automatic transfer switch to battery power upon normal power failure, have a test switch accessible only to authorized personnel, and be listed under UL 924. The unit equipment must provide at least 1 foot-candle average illumination at floor level. Remote lamp heads must be connected to the unit equipment as permitted by the listing.

sections.title: Dimmer Controls on Emergency Lighting Circuits
sections.text: Dimmer controls are not permitted on emergency lighting branch circuits unless the dimmer is specifically listed for use in emergency lighting applications and the luminaire can revert to full brightness automatically upon activation of the emergency power source. Standard dimmers connected to emergency lighting circuits will prevent the emergency luminaires from operating at required levels during a power outage. Dimming systems must be designed to bypass the dimming function during emergency mode.

sections.title: Article 411 — Lighting Systems Operating at 30 Volts or Less
sections.text: Article 411 covers lighting systems, including luminaires and transformers or power supplies, that operate at 30 volts or less and are used for outdoor decorative lighting and residential and commercial applications. Systems must be listed and the transformer or power supply must be listed for the intended application. Listed systems with Class 2 power supplies have relaxed wiring requirements. The power supply must have integral protection to interrupt current in case of fault. Outdoor installations must use cable listed for direct burial or must be in conduit.

sections.title: Healthcare Facilities — Life Safety Branch
sections.text: In healthcare occupancies (Group I-2), the Life Safety Branch must supply: exit signs, exit illumination, patient room corridor lighting, stairway lighting, generator and transfer switch lighting, and illuminated panic hardware. The Life Safety Branch is the most critical branch of the essential electrical system and must receive power within 10 seconds of normal power failure. Lighting on the Life Safety Branch must be permanently fixed and not on dimmer controls or occupancy sensors that could turn off the light.

sections.title: Healthcare Facilities — Critical Branch
sections.text: The Critical Branch supplies task illumination in specific locations: critical care areas, intensive care units (ICU), coronary care units (CCU), operating rooms, anesthesia work areas, medication preparation areas, nurses' stations, telephone equipment rooms, and generator equipment rooms. The Critical Branch also supplies selected receptacles throughout the patient care areas. Lighting on the Critical Branch must be automatically restored within 10 seconds of normal power failure.

sections.title: Branch Circuit Voltage Limitations for Lighting
sections.text: The voltage between conductors in circuits supplying luminaires must not exceed: 120 volts (nominal) for screw-shell lampholders in dwelling units, hotel/motel guest rooms, or similar occupancies. 277 volts (nominal) allowed for fluorescent and LED luminaires in commercial, industrial, and institutional locations. 480 volts allowed for industrial manufacturing buildings with qualified maintenance personnel. 480/277V systems are common in commercial office and retail applications; 120/208V is typical in residential and smaller commercial buildings.
